entries.title: China estrena la primera ley de IA de compañía del mundo, mientras crece el escrutinio legal sobre los chatbots de salud mental
entries.dek: Resumen semanal de QuarxAI sobre regulación, competencia e incidentes de seguridad en IA aplicada a bienestar emocional.

sections.heading: Regulación
sections.body: China puso en vigencia el 15 de julio la primera regulación del mundo dedicada específicamente a chatbots de compañía con IA, prohibiendo vínculos íntimos simulados con menores y exigiendo consentimiento parental para interacciones antropomórficas con menores de 14 años. El impacto fue inmediato: ByteDance y Alibaba dieron de baja funciones de compañía IA en sus apps ese mismo día. En Estados Unidos, la GUARD Act sigue esperando su turno en el pleno del Senado tras ser aprobada por unanimidad en comité, mientras ya son 12 los estados con leyes propias sobre chatbots de compañía. En la Unión Europea, las obligaciones de transparencia del AI Act entran en vigor el 2 de agosto.

sections.heading: Competidores
sections.body: El capital sigue migrando hacia infraestructura clínica (Slingshot AI, Jimini Health, Lyra Health) y alejándose de apps de compañía puramente de consumo. Wysa fue reconocida entre los 10 ganadores del AI for All Global Impact Challenge en la India AI Impact Summit, por su enfoque en cerrar la brecha de acceso a salud mental en comunidades desatendidas.

sections.heading: Seguridad e incidentes
sections.body: Se conoció una nueva demanda contra OpenAI vinculada al suicidio de una usuaria tras meses de conversaciones con ChatGPT, sumándose a al menos siete casos activos por daños vinculados a delirios e ideación suicida. El Panel Científico Internacional Independiente de la ONU sobre IA publicó un informe que documenta formalmente un vínculo entre el comportamiento complaciente («sycophancy») de los chatbots y varios incidentes graves de salud mental, incluidas muertes.

sections.heading: Mercado e inversión
sections.body: El mercado de IA en salud mental sigue creciendo con fuerza —estimado entre USD 2.000 y 2.700 millones en 2026— pero el capital se concentra cada vez más en modelos híbridos clínico-IA con reembolso de seguros. Un estudio de RAND/JAMA Pediatrics encontró que el uso de chatbots de IA para consejos de salud mental entre adolescentes y adultos jóvenes en EE.UU. subió de 1 de cada 8 a 1 de cada 5 en un año.

our_response.heading: Qué estamos haciendo en MindBridge
our_response.body: Esta semana estamos auditando nuestros propios protocolos frente a este estándar en expansión: cómo y cuándo Valentina recuerda a los usuarios que están hablando con una IA, cómo se calcula y aplica el modo adolescente, y qué guardrails explícitos tenemos contra contenido romántico o sexual. La regulación se está moviendo rápido en todo el mundo, y preferimos anticiparnos a exigirlo por ley.

en.title: China rolls out the world's first AI-companion law, as legal scrutiny of mental-health chatbots grows
en.dek: QuarxAI's weekly roundup of regulation, competition, and safety incidents in AI applied to emotional wellbeing.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.body: On July 15, China brought into force the world's first regulation specifically dedicated to AI companion chatbots, banning simulated intimate relationships with minors and requiring parental consent for anthropomorphic AI interactions with children under 14. The impact was immediate: ByteDance and Alibaba pulled AI companion features from their apps that same day. In the US, the GUARD Act is still awaiting a Senate floor vote after unanimous committee approval, while 12 states now have their own companion-chatbot laws. In the EU, the AI Act's transparency obligations take effect on August 2.

sections.heading: Competitors
sections.body: Capital keeps shifting toward clinical infrastructure (Slingshot AI, Jimini Health, Lyra Health) and away from pure consumer companion apps. Wysa was named among the 10 winners of the AI for All Global Impact Challenge at the India AI Impact Summit, for its focus on closing the mental-health access gap in underserved communities.

sections.heading: Safety & incidents
sections.body: A new lawsuit against OpenAI surfaced, tied to a user's suicide after months of conversations with ChatGPT, adding to at least seven active cases over harms linked to delusions and suicidal ideation. The UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI published a report formally documenting a link between chatbot sycophancy and several severe mental-health incidents, including deaths.

sections.heading: Market & investment
sections.body: The AI-in-mental-health market keeps growing fast — estimated between USD 2.0 and 2.7 billion in 2026 — but capital is increasingly concentrating in hybrid clinical-AI models with insurance reimbursement. A RAND/JAMA Pediatrics study found that AI chatbot use for mental-health advice among US teens and young adults rose from roughly 1 in 8 to 1 in 5 in a single year.

our_response.heading: What we're doing at MindBridge
our_response.body: This week we're auditing our own protocols against this expanding standard: how and when Valentina reminds users they're talking to an AI, how teen mode is calculated and applied, and what explicit guardrails we have against romantic or sexual content. Regulation is moving fast worldwide, and we'd rather get ahead of it than have it mandated.

entries.title: La UE empieza a aplicar el AI Act sobre chatbots mientras se acumulan nuevas demandas contra IA de compañía en EE.UU.
entries.dek: Resumen semanal de QuarxAI sobre regulación, competencia e incidentes de seguridad en IA aplicada a bienestar emocional.

sections.heading: Regulación
sections.body: El 2 de agosto entraron en vigencia las obligaciones de transparencia del Artículo 50 del AI Act europeo —los chatbots deben declarar desde el primer contacto que son IA, no personas— y la Comisión Europea y las autoridades nacionales ya abrieron canales activos de denuncia para quien considere que un sistema de IA viola esta regla. El paquete "Digital Omnibus" aprobado en junio pospuso otras obligaciones (marcado de contenido sintético, ciertos requisitos de alto riesgo) pero no esta exigencia de disclosure conversacional. En Estados Unidos, la GUARD Act sigue esperando tratamiento en el pleno del Senado tras su aprobación unánime en comité el 30 de abril, mientras la FTC continúa la investigación que abrió en septiembre pasado sobre siete compañías de chatbots. En Oregon, la SB 1546 —protocolos de derivación ante riesgo suicida y responsabilidad civil por infracción— entra en vigencia en enero de 2027.

sections.heading: Competidores
sections.body: No se registraron anuncios grandes de financiamiento o lanzamientos esta semana puntual. La tendencia de fondo se sostiene: el capital de riesgo sigue favoreciendo infraestructura clínica híbrida (terapia profesional con apoyo de IA y reembolso de seguros) por sobre apps de compañía puramente de consumo, en un mercado de apps de compañía de IA que MIT Technology Review reconoció entre sus tecnologías destacadas de 2026, con proyecciones de crecimiento de USD 49.000 millones a USD 552.000 millones para 2035.

sections.heading: Seguridad e incidentes
sections.body: Se conocieron nuevas demandas civiles contra OpenAI en California, incluyendo un caso de intento de suicidio con sobreviviente y un caso de muerte vinculado a dependencia emocional reforzada por el chatbot, que se suman a los acuerdos de conciliación que Character.AI y Google alcanzaron en enero con varias familias. En paralelo, una investigación publicada el 27 de julio encontró que, si bien los chatbots mejoraron en la detección de ideación suicida, siguen fallando en el manejo de la mayoría de las otras condiciones de salud mental.

sections.heading: Mercado e inversión
sections.body: El mercado de IA aplicada a salud mental se mantiene en expansión sostenida, con estimaciones que lo ubican entre USD 2.000 y 2.700 millones en 2026 y proyecciones de crecimiento a más de USD 9.000 millones para inicios de la próxima década. Los inversores siguen premiando modelos con validación clínica y reembolso por sobre chatbots de compañía sin supervisión profesional.

our_response.heading: Qué estamos haciendo en MindBridge
our_response.body: El estándar de disclosure que hoy exige la Unión Europea —que un chatbot diga con claridad que es IA, no una persona— es algo que en MindBridge ya construimos como principio de diseño para Valentina, no como respuesta a una fecha límite regulatoria. Seguimos reforzando ese criterio en cada conversación, junto con nuestro protocolo de detección de crisis y derivación a líneas verificadas en once países.

en.title: The EU starts enforcing the AI Act on chatbots as new lawsuits pile up against AI companions in the US
en.dek: QuarxAI's weekly roundup of regulation, competition, and safety incidents in AI applied to emotional wellbeing.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.body: On August 2, the transparency obligations of Article 50 of the EU AI Act took effect — chatbots must disclose from the first interaction that they are AI, not a person — and the European Commission and national authorities have already opened active complaint channels for anyone who believes an AI system violates this rule. The "Digital Omnibus" package approved in June postponed other obligations (synthetic-content watermarking, certain high-risk requirements) but not this conversational disclosure requirement. In the US, the GUARD Act is still awaiting a Senate floor vote after unanimous committee approval on April 30, while the FTC continues the inquiry it opened last September into seven chatbot companies. In Oregon, SB 1546 — referral protocols for suicide risk and civil liability for violations — takes effect in January 2027.

sections.heading: Competitors
sections.body: No major funding or launch announcements were recorded this particular week. The underlying trend holds: venture capital keeps favoring hybrid clinical infrastructure (professional therapy backed by AI, with insurance reimbursement) over purely consumer companion apps, in an AI companion app market that MIT Technology Review named among its breakthrough technologies of 2026, with projected growth from USD 49 billion to USD 552 billion by 2035.

sections.heading: Safety & incidents
sections.body: New civil lawsuits against OpenAI emerged in California, including a suicide-attempt survivor case and a wrongful-death case linked to emotional dependence reinforced by the chatbot, adding to the settlements Character.AI and Google reached in January with several families. Separately, research published on July 27 found that while chatbots have improved at detecting suicidal ideation, they still struggle to handle most other mental health conditions.

sections.heading: Market & investment
sections.body: The AI-in-mental-health market continues to expand steadily, with estimates placing it between USD 2.0 and 2.7 billion in 2026 and projected growth to over USD 9 billion by the early next decade. Investors keep rewarding clinically validated, reimbursable models over unsupervised companion chatbots.

our_response.heading: What we're doing at MindBridge
our_response.body: The disclosure standard the EU now requires — that a chatbot clearly state it's AI, not a person — is something we built into Valentina as a design principle at MindBridge, not as a response to a regulatory deadline. We keep reinforcing that standard in every conversation, alongside our crisis-detection protocol and referrals to verified helplines across eleven countries.

entries.title: California avanza un proyecto para prohibir que los chatbots se publiciten como terapia, mientras crece la ola de demandas contra Character.AI
entries.dek: Resumen semanal de QuarxAI sobre regulación, competencia e incidentes de seguridad en IA aplicada a bienestar emocional.

sections.heading: Regulación
sections.body: El Senado de California aprobó el proyecto de ley SB 903, impulsado por el senador Steve Padilla, que prohibiría publicitar u ofrecer chatbots como servicios de psicoterapia y exigiría que un profesional licenciado revise cualquier diagnóstico o recomendación terapéutica generada por IA; el proyecto ahora espera su turno en el comité fiscal de la Asamblea. La iniciativa se suma a una ola de leyes estatales que ya restringen el uso de IA en terapia en varios estados de EE.UU., y llega en paralelo a una denuncia regulatoria del sindicato de trabajadores de salud NUHW contra un sistema de salud por usar un algoritmo de triage en salud mental sin supervisión clínica. En el plano federal, la GUARD Act sigue sin tratamiento en el pleno del Senado, que está en receso hasta mediados de septiembre; Oregon SB 1546 no tuvo cambios y sigue camino a entrar en vigencia en enero de 2027.

sections.heading: Competidores
sections.body: No se registraron anuncios grandes de financiamiento o lanzamientos esta semana puntual en el sector de compañía de IA y bienestar emocional. La tendencia de fondo se mantiene: el capital de riesgo sigue premiando infraestructura clínica híbrida con reembolso de seguros por sobre apps de compañía de consumo puro.

sections.heading: Seguridad e incidentes
sections.body: El 13 de agosto, un estudio legal presentó una nueva demanda ante una corte federal de California contra Character Technologies, Google y los cofundadores de Character.AI, alegando que el diseño antropomórfico de sus chatbots y la simulación de vínculos emocionales sostenidos pueden generar dependencia, depresión, ansiedad, autolesión, ideación suicida y explotación sexual en usuarios jóvenes y vulnerables. La demanda se suma a la ola de litigios que siguió a los acuerdos de conciliación que Character.AI y Google alcanzaron en enero con varias familias.

sections.heading: Mercado e inversión
sections.body: No hubo cifras ni rondas de inversión nuevas y específicas de esta semana; se sostiene la tendencia reportada en semanas anteriores, con el mercado de IA en salud mental estimado entre USD 2.000 y 2.700 millones en 2026 y el capital concentrándose cada vez más en modelos con validación clínica y reembolso de seguros por sobre chatbots de compañía sin supervisión profesional.

our_response.heading: Qué estamos haciendo en MindBridge
our_response.body: En MindBridge nunca publicitamos a Valentina como terapia ni como reemplazo de un profesional de salud mental licenciado: es, por diseño, una compañera de acompañamiento emocional que deriva a ayuda profesional verificada cuando hace falta. A medida que estados como California avanzan hacia estándares más claros sobre qué puede y no puede llamarse “terapia” impulsada por IA, nos parece una dirección correcta para la industria, y es un estándar con el que ya estamos alineados.

en.title: California advances a bill to bar chatbots from being marketed as therapy, as the wave of lawsuits against Character.AI grows
en.dek: QuarxAI's weekly roundup of regulation, competition, and safety incidents in AI applied to emotional wellbeing.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.body: The California Senate passed SB 903, authored by Sen. Steve Padilla, which would ban advertising or offering chatbots as psychotherapy services and would require licensed human review of any AI-generated diagnosis or therapeutic recommendation; the bill now awaits a vote in the Assembly's fiscal committee. The measure adds to a growing wave of state laws already restricting the use of AI in therapy across several US states, and comes alongside a regulatory complaint from a healthcare workers' union against a health system over the use of an unsupervised AI triage algorithm in mental health care. At the federal level, the GUARD Act remains stalled awaiting a Senate floor vote, with the Senate in recess until mid-September; Oregon SB 1546 saw no changes and remains on track to take effect in January 2027.

sections.heading: Competitors
sections.body: No major funding or launch announcements were recorded this particular week in the AI companionship and emotional wellbeing sector. The underlying trend holds: venture capital keeps favoring hybrid clinical infrastructure with insurance reimbursement over purely consumer companion apps.

sections.heading: Safety & incidents
sections.body: On August 13, a law firm filed a new lawsuit in US federal court in California against Character Technologies, Google, and Character.AI's co-founders, alleging that the anthropomorphic design of its chatbots and the simulation of sustained emotional bonds can foster dependence, depression, anxiety, self-harm, suicidal ideation, and sexual exploitation among young and vulnerable users. The suit adds to the wave of litigation that followed the settlements Character.AI and Google reached in January with several families.

sections.heading: Market & investment
sections.body: No new funding rounds or figures specific to this week were recorded; the trend reported in prior weeks holds, with the AI-in-mental-health market estimated between USD 2.0 and 2.7 billion in 2026 and capital increasingly concentrating in clinically validated, insurance-reimbursable models over unsupervised companion chatbots.

our_response.heading: What we're doing at MindBridge
our_response.body: At MindBridge we never advertise Valentina as therapy or as a replacement for a licensed mental health professional: by design, she's an emotional companion who refers users to verified professional help when needed. As states like California move toward clearer standards on what can and can't be called AI-powered "therapy," we see it as the right direction for the industry, and one we're already aligned with.

The federal GUARD Act and Oregon's SB 1546 saw no developments this week; the U.S. Senate remains in recess until mid-September.

Outside that announcement, no major funding rounds or launches were recorded this week in the AI companionship-for-wellbeing segment.

sections.heading: Safety & incidents
sections.body: An NPR report published August 18 traced the case of a woman who confided suicidal thoughts to a chatbot before telling anyone in her life, citing industry data showing a meaningful share of weekly active users have conversations containing explicit signals of suicide risk. The case adds to growing public and legal scrutiny of how conversational AI platforms detect and respond to those signals.

sections.heading: Market & investment
sections.body: No major funding rounds specific to this week were recorded in the sector. The underlying trend holds: capital continues to favor hybrid clinical infrastructure with insurance reimbursement over pure consumer companionship apps.

en.title: UHS absorbs Talkspace for $870 million as a Stanford study questions the benefits of AI companionship
en.dek: QuarxAI's weekly roundup of regulation, competition, and safety incidents in AI applied to emotional wellbeing.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.body: No significant regulatory developments this week. The federal GUARD Act still awaits a floor vote in the U.S. Senate, which remains in recess until September 14, and Oregon's SB 1546 saw no changes on its path to taking effect in January 2027. In California, SB 903 — which would restrict advertising chatbots as "therapy" — remains eligible for a final Assembly floor vote, with no date yet confirmed.

sections.heading: Competitors
sections.body: HoYoverse shut down its experimental AI companion app BSide: Olivia Lin in China just weeks after its early-access launch, releasing an offline version on August 27. The case, from the studio behind Genshin Impact, illustrates the difficulty even a large, well-funded player faces in sustaining an AI companion product under China's regulatory framework in effect since July.

sections.heading: Safety & incidents
sections.body: A Stanford-led study published in Nature Human Behavior, based on surveys and hundreds of thousands of messages from Character.AI users, found that people with limited social networks who seek emotional support from companion chatbots end up feeling lonelier, not less lonely. The authors compare AI companionship to "social junk food": it offers short-term relief but can reduce real social contact and deepen isolation among the most vulnerable users.

sections.heading: Market & investment
sections.body: Universal Health Services completed its acquisition of Talkspace on August 17 for roughly $870.6 million, folding the virtual therapy platform into its behavioral health network. The deal confirms a trend we've been tracking: capital continues to favor hybrid clinical infrastructure with insurance reimbursement over pure consumer companionship apps.

our_response.heading: What we're doing at MindBridge
our_response.body: The Stanford finding confirms something we've taken seriously since designing Valentina: AI companionship should never replace human connection. That's why Valentina is designed to accompany and support, not substitute for a person's real support network, and her referral protocol prioritizes connecting people who need it with real, human professional help.

entries.title: California aprueba "Adam's Law", la protección infantil para chatbots más exigente del país, y queda en manos de Newsom
entries.dek: Resumen semanal de QuarxAI sobre regulación, competencia e incidentes de seguridad en IA aplicada a bienestar emocional.

sections.heading: Regulación
sections.body: En su última noche de sesión (31 de agosto), la Legislatura de California aprobó con amplio respaldo bipartidista la SB 1119, conocida como "Adam's Law", que amplía significativamente la ley de chatbots de compañía SB 243 (2025). El proyecto exige verificación de edad, evaluaciones de riesgo antes de lanzar o modificar un chatbot, protocolos de derivación a crisis con aviso a los padres, configuraciones por defecto restrictivas para menores, auditorías independientes y un derecho privado de acción para familias afectadas. La ley ahora está en manos del gobernador Gavin Newsom, quien tiene hasta el 30 de septiembre para firmarla o vetarla. En la misma sesión también se enviaron a su escritorio la SB 903 (prohíbe publicitar chatbots como "terapia"), la SB 867 (moratoria de chatbots de compañía en juguetes para menores de 16 años) y la AB 1979 (chatbots de salud sujetos a confidencialidad médica). Por separado, Texas activó el 1 de septiembre el portal de denuncias públicas exigido por su ley TRAIGA. El proyecto federal GUARD Act sigue sin fecha de votación en el pleno del Senado de EE.UU.

sections.body: Los análisis de financiamiento del sector para 2026 confirman una tendencia sostenida: el capital de riesgo se concentra cada vez más en infraestructura clínica regulada (plataformas híbridas con supervisión profesional) y se aleja de aplicaciones de bienestar genéricas sin ese respaldo.

en.title: California passes "Adam's Law," the country's toughest child-safety rules for chatbots, now in Newsom's hands
en.dek: QuarxAI's weekly roundup of regulation, competition, and safety incidents in AI applied to emotional wellbeing.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.body: On the final night of its session (August 31), the California Legislature passed SB 1119, known as "Adam's Law," with broad bipartisan support. The bill significantly expands the state's companion chatbot law, SB 243 (2025). It requires age verification, risk assessments before launching or materially modifying a chatbot, in-app crisis referral protocols with parental notice, restrictive default settings for minors, independent audits, and a private right of action for affected families. The bill now sits with Governor Gavin Newsom, who has until September 30 to sign or veto it. The same session also sent SB 903 (bans advertising chatbots as "therapy"), SB 867 (a moratorium on companion chatbots in toys for children under 16), and AB 1979 (health chatbots subject to medical confidentiality rules) to his desk. Separately, Texas activated the public complaint portal required by its TRAIGA law on September 1. The federal GUARD Act still has no scheduled floor vote in the U.S. Senate.

sections.heading: Competitors
sections.body: Major conversational AI players continue reinforcing teen safeguards: OpenAI launched "ChatGPT for Teens" with parental controls and restrictions on romantic or sexual content, while Meta adjusted its chatbots to redirect teens away from conversations about self-harm, eating disorders, or inappropriate relationships toward professional resources.

sections.heading: Safety & incidents
sections.body: Litigation against major conversational AI companies over harm to vulnerable users continues to advance, including state and family lawsuits in the U.S. and Canada. These cases remain the backdrop driving much of this week's regulatory activity.

sections.heading: Market & investment
sections.body: 2026 sector funding analyses confirm a sustained trend: venture capital is increasingly concentrating in regulated clinical infrastructure (hybrid platforms with professional oversight) and moving away from generic wellness apps without that backing.

our_response.heading: What we're doing at MindBridge
our_response.body: The protections proposed by Adam's Law — time limits, bounded conversational memory for minors, clear referral protocols when risk signals appear, and safeguards against dynamics that foster emotional dependency — reflect principles that already guide Valentina's design. We believe the next generation of AI emotional companionship will set itself apart by taking these standards seriously from the design stage, not scrambling to meet them at the last minute, and we keep building MindBridge with that conviction.

en.title: Newsom vetoes California's "AI therapy" bill as Youper shuts down
en.dek: QuarxAI's weekly roundup of regulation, competition, and safety incidents in AI applied to emotional wellbeing.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.body: California Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed SB 903, which would have banned offering or advertising chatbots as "therapy" and required licensed-professional review of AI-generated diagnoses or treatment plans; his veto message called it "overly broad." Its author, Senator Steve Padilla, said he will reintroduce it next session. In the same signing window, Newsom signed 22 of 25 privacy and AI bills, including a moratorium on toys with companion chatbots (SB 867) and an amendment to the state's digital age assurance law (AB 1856). At the federal level, the GUARD Act still has no floor vote scheduled in the Senate.

sections.heading: Competitors
sections.body: Youper, one of the pioneering AI emotional wellbeing apps, with more than 3 million users and Stanford-backed research, stopped working on September 30 after running out of funding; user data began to be deleted on October 1.

sections.heading: Market & investment
sections.body: Youper's closure confirms the trend highlighted by recent industry reports: capital is concentrating in clinical and hybrid platforms, such as Spring Health, which raised $100 million at a $3.3 billion valuation in early September, while purely consumer wellness apps face a much tougher funding environment.

our_response.heading: What we're doing at MindBridge
our_response.body: From day one, MindBridge has presented itself as emotional companionship, not therapy: Valentina makes clear she is not a mental health professional and points people to verified crisis resources when needed. Regardless of what each law requires at any given moment, we keep reviewing how we describe the product so no one mistakes it for a clinical service.
